newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: After new premier, S.Korea to get new economic team.
newsitem.headline: After new premier, S.Korea to get new economic team.

text.p: After replacing his prime minister on Tuesday, South Korean President Kim Young-sam is likely to dump economic ministers in a cabinet reshuffle on Wednesday, newspapers and economists said.
Kim sacked Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung to take responsiblity for a loans scandal involving bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co.
Lee was replaced by a former mayor of Seoul, Koh Kun.

The Hanbo affair, which rocked the banking system and cast further gloom over a slowing economy, is likely to cost finance minister Han Seung-soo his job after just eight months, according to ministry officials, who declined to be identified.
Newspapers speculated that six or seven economy-related ministers would go, including the ministers for Construction and Transportation and Science and Technology.
Ministry portfolios related to political and foreign affairs and security are widely seen as remaining unchanged to ensure policy stability at a time of instability in neighbouring North Korea.

Leading dailies were divided over whether Trade Minister Ahn Kwang-koo would hold on to his job in the face of a worrying trade deficit and criticism of the ministry's role in the crisis that brought down Hanbo Steel.
Figures released on Monday showed the customs-cleared deficit for February widened to $2.1 billion from a shortfall of $1.6 billion a year earlier.
The trade ministry was behind a decision to approve Hanbo's construction of a new steel mill that some economists regard as a white elephant.

The Chosun Ilbo and Dong A Ilbo dailies both picked Kang Kyong-sik, a parliamentary member of the ruling New Korea Party as the most likely candidate for finance minister, one of two deputy prime ministers in the cabinet.
Kang served in the position in 1982 under the presidency of former military strongman Chun Doo Hwan. He later became Chun's chief secretary.
The Hankook Ilbo newspaper speculated the next finance minister would be Lee Sang-Deuk, another ruling party lawmaker with a business background.
From 1983 to 1988 Lee was president of Kolon International, the trading arm of the Kolon Group, a top-30 industrial conglomerate.

Several papers named as an outside possibility for the finance job Kim Mahn-je, the chairman of Pohang Iron and Steel (POSCO) the world's second largest steelmaker. Kim is also a former finance minister.
"Any new finance minister should know the economy both in theory and reality," said a finance ministry official who asked not to be identified.
"He should be a man who can understand the public mind and be able to push forward government economic policy."
Economists said they did not expect much from the widely-expected reshuffle.
"There are no quick remedies to cure our economy," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Economic and Research.
He said the most pressing task for the new economic management team would be to restore crediblity to the banking system and put to rest the Hanbo scandal.
